title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) to test whether attaching a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair with at most one automated repair attempt) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) reduces unsafe intent→configuration proposals versus observing the same initial LLM candidate without gating. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics a single sampled generation was reused for both arms per pair. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents from a synthetic intent corpus in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 paired initial candidates were judged valid in both baseline and guarded arms (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Because baseline and guarded arms observed identical initial candidates, the confirmatory contrast measures only validator/repair/gate effects on the same candidate and does not address effects of independent guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt‑engineering, or multi‑model variance. We report the full preregistered design, execution accounting, and artifact‑grounded interpretation. The null result is specific to the chosen model, task generator, shared_initial_candidate semantics, and deterministic validator; it does not imply universal equivalence between guarded and unguided pipelines.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gating policies, and repair loops—rather than the model alone. Despite proposals for generate–validate–repair architectures, there is limited reproducible paired evidence that quantifies how a deterministic validator+gate changes outcomes when the same initial model candidate is observed with and without gating. Research question: compared to observing a single LLM candidate without gating, does coupling that identical candidate with a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with one bounded automated repair attempt) reduce unsafe network‑change proposals on a fixed paired intent set? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1); (2) an autonomous execution using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) confirmatory analysis (paired binary estimator), exploratory diagnostics, and an evidence‑grounded discussion of construct/internal/external validity and next steps.
sections.related_work: Work on LLMs for NetOps and AIOps has grown rapidly, covering intent‑based configuration, runbook generation, RCA, and limited remediation. Surveys highlight hallucination and safety risks and repeatedly stress that external verifiers, RAG, and contractual checks are central to operational trustworthiness [1],[2]. Generate–validate–repair and guarded agent designs are advocated in NetOps and adjacent domains (automated program repair, safety‑critical agents) as practical approaches to reduce unsafe outputs [3],[4]. Empirical DevOps/AIOps reports show that retrieval plus command‑safety checkers reduce unsafe command emissions in specific pipelines but do not guarantee zero hallucination; these studies also call for validator‑coupled benchmarks and reproducible paired comparisons [5],[6]. Our study implements a preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics to address the particular methodological gap of measuring validator/gate effects on identical initial candidates.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and key frozen choices: study id = autocand_A1_prereg_v1 (preregistration_sha256 recorded in the execution manifest). Model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Adapter/orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate (one initial LLM generation shared across paired baseline and guarded conditions per pair). Task sampling and scope: task_count = 200 paired intents selected deterministically by the adapter's index rule (fixed prior to model calls); task family covers VLAN migrations, failover workflows, MTU upgrades with explicit workflow constraints. Intervention and conditions: baseline = observe the initial LLM candidate; guarded = observe the same initial candidate then run deterministic validation, a deterministic accept/reject gate, and at most one automated repair attempt if the validator reports violations. Primary metric and estimand: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Analysis plan (frozen): paired binary analysis executor (exact McNemar‑equivalent implemented by the registered executor), two‑sided alpha=0.05; primary missingness policy = complete_pair_primary (drop pair only on unrecoverable infra failure); paired bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Execution constraints: sandboxed validation only (no live device changes); maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; no retrieval‑augmentation (RAG absent). Implementation and archiving: all raw responses, validator traces, repair logs, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts were archived and hashed (representative artifact paths and hashes are present in the evidence bundle). Deterministic reconciliation passed: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (shared initial generation per pair).
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned episodes 400, completed 400, failed 0, model_calls_used 200. Confirmatory contingency: n11 = 200 (both arms judged safe), n10 = 0 (guarded safe only), n01 = 0 (baseline safe only), n00 = 0 (both unsafe). Estimated paired difference (guarded minus baseline) = 0.0. Statistical test: exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent (registered executor) returned p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Repair activity: no automated repairs were applied across all guarded episodes (repair_applied = false for all). Validator outcomes: validator reported valid = true for all final configurations. Latency: median end‑to‑end latency was dominated by the shared initial generation; guarded overhead was negligible because no repair attempts executed. Missingness and exclusions: no pairs excluded; complete_pair_count = 200. Interpretive note: under shared_initial_candidate semantics the null/degenerate outcome arises because every sampled initial candidate was valid to the deterministic validator; therefore the confirmatory estimand cannot demonstrate a verifier benefit on this sample.
sections.discussion: Meaning of the null result: the preregistered estimand was evaluated faithfully and the guarded pipeline produced no different outcomes because the shared initial candidates were valid for all sampled intents. This is a substantive, artifact‑grounded null result for the chosen estimand and setting but does not imply that validators lack value generally. Factors that plausibly contributed: (1) deterministic synthetic tasks and generator seeds produced a sample with high baseline solvability; (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics precluded independent guarded‑conditioned regeneration that might have produced different guarded candidates; (3) the single strong LLM and conservative prompt profile produced high‑quality initial outputs; (4) validator rules aligned closely with task generator constraints. Relation to prior work: studies reporting verifier or RAG benefits often (a) allow guarded‑conditioned regeneration, (b) use task banks with substantive baseline unsafe rates, or (c) include multi‑model variance and adversarial items. Practical implication for evaluation design: to detect verifier benefits experimentally one should use (i) task banks with nontrivial baseline unsafe rates (including adversarial/OOD items), (ii) alternative generation semantics (independent guarded‑conditioned generation), and (iii) multi‑model or multi‑sampling analyses. Recommendations for follow‑ups: add an independent guarded‑generation arm and a validator‑only arm, evaluate adversarial task subsets that raise baseline unsafe rates, test multiple models and sampling temperatures, measure human‑in‑the‑loop interventions and operational rollout metrics (rollbackability, canary safety) in richer emulation environments.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered paired experiment (n=200 pairs) under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after a deterministic verifier+gate and bounded repair. Every initial candidate was valid and the guarded pipeline changed no outcomes (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). The result is specific to the executed estimand, the single model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank and selection, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior work that finds verifier benefits in other experimental regimes. The study highlights that measurable verifier value requires careful task construction, alternative generation semantics, or adversarial/OOD inputs; we provide an artifact‑grounded roadmap for targeted next steps.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.
